SpaceX cumulative orbital deliveries now exceed the total from every other launch provider
in history.
The gap stems from reusable Falcon 9 first stages that return to landing platforms or ground
pads after each flight. No other operator has matched the flight rate or payload capacity
achieved so far. The company's Starlink missions continue at high cadence and keep pushing the
total higher. Future Starship flights could widen the margin further once they enter regular service.
SpaceX is also preparing a dis-shaped reentry vehicle called the Starfall capsule.
For a demonstration flight, the capsule is sized to return small batches of materials processed
in microgravity. No prior commercial reentry system has offered routine, low-cost,
sample return from orbit. Engineers are targeting specific performance metrics during the upcoming test.
Speculation continues about whether a payload was dropped from a recent related launch.
Estimated splash-down timing for the Starfall demo has been discussed in tracking updates.
The capsule is being included in counts of 2026 orbital launch activity.
From launch dominance on Earth to what that capability might enable on another planet.
Researchers have mapped the measurements needed to judge whether warming Mars is feasible.
The plan focuses on releasing greenhouse gases or deploying orbital mirrors to raise surface
temperatures enough for liquid water. Key unknowns include how much carbon dioxide remains
trapped in the polar caps and regolith. Data from current orbiters and future landers will feed
into climate models that test each scenario. The study provides a clear checklist rather than
claiming success is assured. While engineers plan how to warm Mars, scientists are still debating whether
life was ever there. Discussion threads are revisiting the 1976 Viking lander biology experiments that
tested for metabolic activity in Martian soil. The original results remain ambiguous, with some scientists
still arguing the labeled release tests showed signs of life while others attribute the signals to
chemistry. Recent posts compare those early data with modern instruments such as Perseverance,
Sherlock, and Pixel. Contributors note that sample handling differences between 1976 and today
limit direct comparisons. The conversation centers on what a new dedicated life detection mission
would need to resolve the question. The same planet that sparks life detection debates is also
revealing its deep interior history. Researchers at the University of Oxford have identified signs of
enormous Earth-like, magnetic systems that once existed deep beneath the Martian surface.
The findings challenge the long-held view that plate tectonics are required for such complex geology.
Data from orbital instruments revealed layered structures consistent with repeated episodes of large
scale melting and intrusion. These hidden systems would have shaped the planet's crust and mantle
over billions of years. Follow-up studies will examine whether similar features appear in other
regions of Mars. Curiosity is shifting its focus on Mount Sharp after orbital images showed texture
differences in the terrain ahead. The rover will drive a short distance toward a smoother patch
identified from orbit. That site may expose mineral assemblages distinct from the rougher bedrock
studied recently. Onboard instruments will measure chemistry and texture to check whether the change
records shifts in ancient lake or wind conditions. The next planning cycle will decide whether to pause
for contact science or keep climbing toward higher strata. Mars is not the only world whose interior
models may need revision. New interior models suggest Uranus and Neptune could host hot, rocky magma
layers rather than the traditional water ammonia ises. Voyager 2 fly by data from 1986 and 1989
remain the only direct measurements leaving room for alternative compositions. Revised equations of
state show that silicate mantles under high pressure and temperature could match the observed
densities and magnetic fields. The shift would change how scientists interpret heat flow and atmospheric
dynamics on both worlds. Future orbiter missions will test these predictions through gravity and
magnetic measurements. While outer planet models shift, astronomers are getting sharper views of our
own galaxy center. The Euclid mission released its widest and sharpest view yet of the galactic center
in visible wavelengths. The image covers a crowded field packed with stars and dust that ground
telescopes struggle to resolve. Euclid's wide field camera captured the data during routine survey
operations. Scientists will use the mosaic to map stellar populations and dust lands across the
inner galaxy. Future data releases will add near infrared layers to the same region. Another
telescope is also delivering unprecedented star counts this time in an edge on galaxy. Infrared
observations pierce thick lanes of dust to map the thin disk and bold structure of an unnamed
edge on spiral. The census provides a rare side on census of stellar populations across the full
radial extent. This view helps calibrate models of how dust and stars are distributed in galaxies
viewed at other angles. Future papers will compare the star counts against simulations of disc
formation. From distant galaxies to our own solar system's visitors, a newly analyzed object
that passed through the inner solar system last year shows a composition consistent with formation
during the universe's peak star forming era. Spectral data suggests the comet originated in a cold
dense cloud within a stellar system that was ejected early in galactic history. Its ices and dust
differ markedly from anything formed in our own solar system. Astronomers are using the object to
test models of how planet testimoles are scattered between stars. Follow-up observations with
additional facilities are planned to refine the age estimate. While ancient objects pass through,
Canada is charting its own future role in space. A new analysis argues Canada can expand its role
through targeted investments in robotics and earth observation. The report highlights existing
strengths in satellite technology and astronaut contributions. It recommends closer coordination
between government, universities, and industry. No specific funding figures are attached to the
proposals. Next steps depend on upcoming federal budget decisions. Japan has donated $23.6 million
toward Paraguay's first space technology center. The funding will support construction and initial
operations of the new facility. Paraguay has not previously operated its own dedicated space
technology infrastructure. The donation builds on existing bilateral cooperation in science and
technology. Local teams will gain access to training and equipment through the center. Implementation
timelines will be set once construction contracts are finalized. Before their flights, Apollo crews
practice sampling and traverse planning in Alaska's Valley of 10,000 smokes. The landscape,
shaped by volcanic ash flows, gave astronauts experience identifying rock types and structures
quickly. Those exercises shaped how crews later documented samples returned from the moon.
Archival photos and audio from the sessions are now part of a new public exhibit.
The training underscored the value of field geology skills for lunar surface operations.
Space Shuttle Endeavour has been placed on permanent display in California.
The orbiter joins other retired vehicles in a museum setting that highlights its flight history. Visitors
can now view the vehicle alongside artifacts from its missions. The display preserves the engineering
details of the reusable spacecraft design. Planning for the installation drew on records from the entire
shuttle program. From national strategy to a quick look at other notable items this week. Researchers
have linked specific reentry events to sudden spikes in atmospheric metal concentrations.
The data come from ground-based sampling that captured elevated levels of elements commonly used
in spacecraft construction. These measurements show how material from returning stages disperses
at altitudes where it can interact with the stratosphere. Follow-up studies aim to quantify how
frequently such injections occur as launch rates rise. A satellite tracking tool now includes
an option that removes artificial magnification so objects appear at their real sizes.
Users can select the International Space Station and watch the view zoom out until the station
shrinks to a single pixel against the globe. The update incorporates accurate three-dimensional
models for the International Space Station, Hubble, Tiangong, and thousands of star-link satellites.
Real-time propagation still runs on cellist-track data, but the visual now matches the physical
spacing of objects in orbit. Season 53, Episode 7 of the Long Running Science Series focuses on
current lunar exploration architecture. The program covers lander development, surface operations,
and the role of commercial partners in establishing a presence. Interviews highlight engineering
challenges that must be solved before crews can stay for extended periods. Archival footage from
earlier programs is woven in to show how far planning has advanced. One company is exploring whether
oysters could serve as biological water filters for future astronauts. The approach would use the
shellfish to remove contaminants from recycled water aboard spacecraft or habitats. Laboratory tests
have shown promising filtration rates under controlled conditions. Engineers are evaluating how
such a system could integrate with existing life support hardware. The concept remains an early
development, but could reduce reliance on chemical filters. Keep an eye on upcoming federal budget
